name: smol_str (inline immutable string)
baseline: String for short, mostly immutable strings
verdict_reason: An independent test confirms the allocation win: loading 1,000 US city records, SmolStr cut allocation events from 2,017 to 23 because almost every name fits inline. The test ran in a debug build with 2020 versions and published speed results only as charts, so the evidence covers allocations and memory, not time.
tier_reason: Independent article with numbers in text; allocation counts and peak memory only, measured in a debug build.
claimed_speedup: Allocation events 2017 with String vs 23 with SmolStr; peak memory 82.7 KB vs 73.9 KB for 1000 records.
workload: Deserializing 1,000 JSON records of US city names with serde_json, counting allocations with a tracking global allocator.
platforms: All Rust targets; no_std with alloc
one_liner: Immutable string type that stores up to 23 bytes inline and clones in O(1); far fewer allocations than String for short tokens.
how_it_is_fast: SmolStr is the size of a String but stores short strings (and runs of newlines followed by spaces) inline, so creating them allocates nothing. Longer strings live in an Arc<str>, so clone is a reference-count increment instead of a copy.
use_it_when: Many short, immutable strings such as identifiers, tokens or names that are created once and cloned often.
skip_it_when: Strings are mutated after creation: SmolStr is immutable; compact_str or String fit better.
Strings are mostly longer than the inline limit and rarely cloned: the Arc adds a small constant cost over String.
caveats: Measured in a debug build; allocation counts do not depend on optimization level, but no optimized timing numbers are in text.
Article dates from 2020 and used smol_str 0.1.15; the current crate is 0.3.x and stores up to 23 bytes inline.
The standalone repository is archived; the crate now lives in the rust-analyzer repository, which is where the last-commit date comes from. Stars are the archived repository's.
rosetta-rs/string-rosetta-rs dropped smol_str from its comparison in favor of ecow.
tradeoffs: Immutable API; any change builds a new string.
Heap strings are Arc-backed, adding atomic reference counting.

evidence.quote: and the number of allocations fell from 2017 to just 23!
